items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then you worked with Charlie Barnet. You recorded with him a year later and sat in with his band, playing trumpet.

ctx.x: . . . and talk about . . . oh, before we do that, we’re still working with 1933 and your recordings, and it struck me, we mentioned there was one integrated session of the Chocolate Dandies with that title—anachronistic title, oddly enough; it was an integrated band—and later that year you also recorded with Mez Mezro and his orchestra. I believe that was an offshoot of some grandiose idea he had to tour with an interracial group, which never came to fruition, but this was sort of a spin-off from that. Then you…
[unclear], was that one of the songs?

items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: back in '34 when I had Garnet Clark playing piano up there and Benny Carter sitting back in the trumpet section on certain nights

ctx.x: The reason probably was pressure, wasn't it, or was it?

Well, you see, I had never had any pressure that way, because I had never tried to do it, and I never got any pressure back in '34 when I had Garnet Clark playing piano up there and Benny Carter sitting back in the trumpet section on certain nights. I never heard a word from the management about it. You see, I never ran into this, and somehow or other I tend to find some of these stories must be greatly exaggerated. Maybe -- maybe these curious people that I'm talking about were met with some kind of antagonism,…

Do you suppose that maybe your attitude had something to do with it, that you took it or accepted it as curiosity, and therefore it didn't go in the wrong direction, whereas someone else took it as hostility?

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I know that I recorded one time with Charlie Barnett's big band on trumpet in some studio downtown.

ctx.x: And I don't know about the network
studios, but I know that I recorded one time with Charlie Barnett's big band on trumpet in some studio downtown.

I think this is the case, as perhaps frequently happens, that journalists, jazz critics and historians are looking for firsts, looking for all kinds of sharp distinctions when something -- as we discussed earlier -- when something began, and when another thing began, and maybe it's a big exaggerated.
